DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

The arithmetic in Table 1 and the £810/week figure check out, and the three proposed prices do sit below each competitor midpoint. But the risotto decision rests on a misreading of the data, and the projected effect leaves out a cost increase the paper itself reports. Both need fixing before this goes to the owners.

## Major issues

**1. The risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu, not the weakest.**
Table 1 shows risotto at 80%, the best of any dish. In cash terms it earns £11.20 a plate, more than the curry (£10.90) or the burger (£10.80). The paper's own data contradicts the justification in 5.2.

The replacement also makes things worse. Specials currently run at 64%. A seasonal special at £14.00 with a typical specials margin would cost roughly £200 a week in gross profit compared with the risotto. If the risotto is your main or only vegetarian main, removing it also risks losing group bookings, which is a separate issue.

If there's a real case for dropping it (for example kitchen time, wastage, or the fact that it ties with specials for lowest volume), make that case instead. As written, 5.2 should be reversed or rewritten.

**2. The projection ignores the 12% beef increase in Section 4.**
The £810 is extra revenue at constant cost. But the burger and steak are the dishes facing the beef rise from the same date. If beef makes up most of their food cost:
- Steak: about +£1.25 a plate × 120 = roughly £150 a week
- Burger: about +£0.50 a plate × 260 = roughly £130 a week

That could take up to about £280 a week off the gain, so the net figure is nearer **£530/week (about £27,500/year)**, not £42,000. Most of the steak's £2.00 increase just covers its beef cost.

**3. The "about 71%" margin claim doesn't survive points 1 and 2.**
Using Table 1 (and assuming specials average about £15), the current main-course margin is about 69.4%. The price rises alone take it to about 70.8%, which matches the paper. But once you add the beef costs (about 69.2%) and the risotto swap (about 68%), mains margin goes *down*. That means it doesn't help restore the 70% target in Section 1.

## Moderate issues

**4. The loyalty argument cuts both ways.**
Having 60% repeat guests means most customers *know* the old prices and will notice. That's not evidence they will absorb the increase. "Not drawing attention to the increases" (Section 6) is less likely to work with regulars.

**5. "Volumes hold" is assumed, not tested.**
A break-even volume figure would be more persuasive. For example, at £17.50 fish and chips can lose about 8% of volume (310 → about 285 plates) before gross profit falls. Showing this for each dish would turn "we expect volumes to hold" into a measurable risk.

**6. The monitoring baseline is seasonally skewed.**
January and February are usually the quietest months, so April and May volumes may rise even if price rises are costing you trade. Compare against the same weeks last year, or track each dish's *share* of mains. Also set a trigger: what drop, over how long, leads to what action? Without that it isn't really an early warning.

**7. The risk evidence is thin.**
- "No visible effect on bookings" in 2024: bookings don't capture changes in covers per booking, dish mix, or walk-ins.
- "Weekday lunch is a small share": not quantified. Friday and Saturday dinner are "just under half", so the other half is spread across the remaining sessions. Give the figure.

**8. Fish cost risk is understated.**
Fish and chips is your top seller and its price rise does the most work in the projection. Section 4 calls fish prices "volatile" but the risks section doesn't mention it.

## Minor issues

- **Section 8** says "six trading days a week", but Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five.
- **Annualising at ×52** assumes no closures. Note any closure weeks.
- **Section 1** is about overall food margin (all courses), but the paper only covers mains. Say what mains margin is needed to reach 70% overall, given starters and desserts.

## Comments on the author's summary

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Grounded in till, competitor and supplier data | Yes, but the supplier data isn't carried into the projection |
| Each dish stays below competitor midpoint | Correct (£17.50 < £17.98; £16.00 < £16.50; £28.00 < £29.50) |
| £810/week, about £42k/year | Arithmetic correct, but gross of the beef increase; net is closer to £27–28k |
| Main-course margin lifts to about 71% | Only before beef costs and the risotto swap; with them, about 68% |
| Risotto has the weakest margin | **Incorrect.** It has the strongest (80%) |
| Low-risk and well evidenced | Prices are reasonable; the risotto proposal and the profit figures need rework |

## Suggested fixes

1. Drop or rewrite 5.2.
2. Restate 5.3 net of beef costs, with break-even volumes for each dish.
3. Fix the "six days" error.
4. Change the monitoring baseline to the same period last year and add action triggers.

The price increases themselves look defensible. It's the supporting numbers and the menu-mix change that need work.
